Pete Hegseth has confirmed the execution of a man convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting by firing squad will be livestreamed.
Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.
Secretary of War Mr Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, had told the Human Events Daily program broadcast by Real America's Voice that he planned to make Hasan's execution public.
One Pentagon official told reporters: "The Secretary is correct. It will be livestreamed. Details will follow."
Mr Hegseth said deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1pm, the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting, was a "no-brainer."
He continued: "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public.
"Because people need to understand that...there's serious consequences for these types of things."
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3."
A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan.
He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.
Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad, something President Donald Trump did on Mr Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon disclosed on Monday.
Mr Hegseth said: "It hasn't been since World War II that we've done that. Well, kind of like the mentality we had in World War II."
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
President Donald Trump approved the shooting at the instruction of Pete Hegseth
|REUTERS
The White House has declined to say whether President Trump supported the livestreaming of the execution, instead referring questions to the Pentagon.
The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging.
The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the centre reported.
The White House has declined to confirm whether Donald Trump supports the livestreaming
| REUTERS
At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.
Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.
The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out.
Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalised.
Her lawyers said on Wednesday she awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital.
Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

US to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution: Pentagon
October 9, 2026
The execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Ford Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed, the US military said Thursday.
The confirmation came a day after US Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth had said Hasan's execution, which is slated for December 3, would be done in "public."
Pentagon officials added that more details on the execution would follow.
What did Pete Hegseth say about Nidal Hasan's execution?
In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said Wednesday that Hasan would get "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
Hegseth was speaking to right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which ended a nearly 10-month deployment on Thursday.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things," Hegseth said.
Hasan's execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and will be the first to be done by firing squad since World War II.
Hegseth added: "I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win."
What do we know about the Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan?
US Army psychiatrist Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.
A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.
During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.
The announcement that Hasan will be executed by firing squad comes amid the fallout of the botched execution of Christa Pike.

sources.news_title: Hegseth vows public firing-squad execution for Fort Hood shooter
sources.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a mass shooting in 2009, would be visible to the public.
“He’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be,” Hegseth said on the Real America’s Voice network on Thursday. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Fort Hood Soldier Readiness Center in Killeen, Texas, killing 13 and wounding 32 others before he was subdued on November 5, 2009. He was sentenced by a military court to death after confessing to the shooting.
The shooting occurred at the height of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and Hasan, who is Muslim, had become radicalized against the U.S. role in the conflict. He was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan later that month.
Hasan will be executed on December 3 at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1 pm Texas time, to mirror the date and timing that the shooting took place 17 years ago, Hegseth said.
President Donald Trump approved the execution last week — a decision Hegseth described on Thursday as a “no brainer.” Soldiers with rifles will carry out the execution, he said.
Executing someone by firing squad, and doing so in public view, would mark an unprecedented event in modern U.S. history. The last U.S. military execution came 65 years ago, and the last by firing squad is believed to have been carried out in 1945, when an Army private was shot for desertion during World War II in France.
The final documented public execution in the U.S. took place nine years earlier, in 1936, when a man convicted of rape was hanged in Kentucky in front of thousands of spectators.

Hegseth says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be ‘public’
An official at the Pentagon told Al Jazeera that former US Army Major Nidal Hassan’s execution would be ‘livestreamed’.
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the execution of a former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in Texas will be publicly available to watch.
In an interview with the media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Hegseth was asked about President Donald Trump’s recent order to use a firing squad to execute Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of the 2009 shooting.
The secretary said he approved of the decision, calling it a “no-brainer”.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth told interviewer Jack Posobiec. “Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
Hegseth added that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (19:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place.
Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for the shooting.
The former Army major walked into an army processing centre on the Texas base, shouted “Allahu akbar” (God is greatest) and opened fire on fellow military members waiting to get medical attention.
Hasan’s execution required approval from Hegseth and Trump, who authorised the use of the firing squad on Monday.
An official with the Defense Department told Al Jazeera that Hasan’s execution would be “livestreamed”, adding that more details would come soon.
It is not clear from Hegseth’s remarks whether troops, spectators or US military officials would be present in person for the execution. US Army regulation states that at least two media outlets should be selected as witnesses.
No state or federal execution has ever been televised in the US. The last public execution in the country took place more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky, on August 14, 1936.
The last time a US military execution was conducted by firing squad was in 1945, for desertion during World War II.
When asked to comment on Hegseth’s remarks – and whether Trump would view the execution – the White House referred Al Jazeera to the Pentagon.
The Trump administration announced it would add death by firing squad as an acceptable method for federal executions in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.

Washington DC [US], October 9 (ANI): US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday (local time) said the public would be able to watch the execution of former US Army Major Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, saying he would be executed by a firing squad of soldiers at the military installation.
Speaking to Real America's Voice, Hegseth described the decision as a “no-brainer” and said the execution would take place at Fort Hood on December 3, a Thursday, at 1 pm, the time when Hasan carried out the attack.
“No-brainer. Execution by firing squad. Army major betrays his country, radical Islamist kills a bunch of Americans at Fort Hood. Of course we're going to do it at Fort Hood. We're going to do it on a Thursday. We're going to do it at 1:00, which is when he did it. And it's going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad,” Hegseth said.
He said the execution would be made public so people could understand the consequences of such attacks.
“We haven't done this since WWII…He’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be. And we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public because people need to understand that what this is, there's serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
According to Axios, the US has not held a public execution in 90 years, and Hegseth’s remarks raise questions about how the military would allow people to watch.
Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3 at Fort Hood, Axios reported.
Axios reported that the Pentagon says the execution will be livestreamed, but did not name where the stream will be hosted. The Pentagon currently posts speeches and videos on X and YouTube, Axios noted.
The Department of Defence declined to comment on Hegseth’s remarks, leaving questions about how the public could watch the execution, according to Axios. Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice News this week, said, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” Officials in the Pentagon clarified on Thursday (US time) that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of an execution – let alone one as violent as a firing squad – has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the United States, especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which is a legal request for a court to review the legality of someone’s detention, and could significantly delay the execution, experts on military law said.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specialising in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails.
Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike’s botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.
When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and militaryness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasise – the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raised a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, “I don’t recall a situation in which it was instituted by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government,” she said.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was sceptical that the administration had given second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action. Those warnings preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran at the end of February.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on January 14. “It’s stopping, and there’s no plan for executions.”
He repeated that on January 20 at a White House press briefing. Slightly more than a month later in his State of the Union address, Trump said, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence”.
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief simply replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on November 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunisations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defence during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralysed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behaviour at trial, he may not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan began his portion of the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence.
As the trial progressed, those suspicions grew. The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defence and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed him telling military mental health workers that he could “still be a martyr” if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, spoke with Hasan on Wednesday but is barred from offering much detail about that conversation. He is not representing Hasan in his criminal case but said he’s worried about his physical health under the plan laid out by officials, and that Hasan has not yet had access to legal counsel.
Galligan said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain but no attorney from either the Trial Defence Service or from his civilian defence when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution. Galligan called that a breach of Army regulations.
A spokeswoman for the Army said on Thursday that multiple attempts were made to contact Trial Defence Service attorneys, saying they made every reasonable effort and adhered to policy.
The spokeswoman also said Hasan has not been kept from contacting and communicating with his counsel.
Hegseth said the military had not executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was executed by hanging.
The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the Death Penalty Information Centre reported.
Amnesty International said in its report on executions in 2025 that it knew of at least 17 public executions – 11 in Iran and 6 in Afghanistan.

Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says

The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
An official from the Defense Department told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said on Thursday. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The shooting on 5 November 2009 took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
At court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
There is no modern-era precedent for having a public execution, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
"It looks to me designed to be a grotesque spectacle," he said. "It's an unprecedented decision in the modern era, and so it is on uncertain legal terrain," he added.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution.
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened.
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says.
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-redistricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing.
It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content.

Hegseth Calls Execution a 'No-Brainer'
Hegseth described the decision to execute Hasan by firing squad as a “no-brainer” and said the execution would take place at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1 p.m., which he said was the time Hasan carried out the attack.

Army Rules Limit Who Can Witness Executions
Army Regulation 190-55 governs who may witness military executions, and it does not provide for unrestricted public attendance.
Pentagon officials clarified Thursday that Hasan’s execution will be livestreamed, with more details to follow, according to The Associated Press. It remains unclear whether the public will be allowed to attend in person.

The Army said Hasan's execution would be conducted in accordance with the regulation.
Newsweek reached out to the Pentagon for additional information. The White House declined to comment and referred inquiries to the Department of Defense.
A Rare Return to the Firing Squad
Firing squads have been used only rarely in modern U.S. executions. Several states allow the method, and South Carolina carried out a firing-squad execution last year, the first in the country in 15 years.
An execution by a military firing squad, however, would be especially rare. The U.S. military has not carried out a death sentence in more than six decades.

No legal execution in the United States has been broadcast live to the public, making the Pentagon's announcement that Hasan's execution will be livestreamed an unusual development in the country's history of capital punishment.
